title: Which parts of a conversation reveal what someone is thinking?
text:
In brief. I had six studies, recorded over roughly 20 years by different research teams with different designs, in which observers watched recorded conversations and wrote down what they thought a speaker was thinking. The speakers had written down what they were thinking too. The job was to find out which parts of the conversation predicted each. I transcribed 74 hours of video, split it into utterances, labeled each one, scored how closely it matched each written guess and each written thought, and modeled that score over the course of the conversation. The clearest single result: suggestions (advice, recommendations, proposals) tracked what speakers were actually thinking more closely, on average, than any other kind of utterance, questions included. Two broader patterns held across all six studies. What was said most recently predicts both the guess and the truth. Which person said it makes no difference.

title: Which parts of a conversation reveal what someone is thinking?
text:
The problem
Earlier studies asked whether words mattered by muting the audio and checking whether accuracy dropped. It did. Nobody had asked which words, said when, by whom. Work on conversation also treats questions as the move that draws out what someone is thinking (Graesser & Person, 1994), so questions were my best guess for the most revealing utterances. The same question shows up in industry under other names: which part of a support call predicts the CSAT score, which minutes of a sales call predict the close, which turns of a user interview a summary should keep. Answering it takes a pipeline that turns recorded talk into a measurement, and a way to know how far to trust each step.

title: Which parts of a conversation reveal what someone is thinking?
text:
The data






Note



Six studies spanning roughly 20 years of recordings. 74 hours of video, 1,346 observers, 956 speakers, 11,906 written guesses, between 3,300 and 68,300 utterances per study. Two studies were interview-style (many observers judging a few recorded speakers); four were live two-person conversations where each person later judged the other. Transcripts and written responses are IRB-restricted and stay in the lab. This page shows model summaries only. The code runs end to end on simulated data with the same structure.

title: Which parts of a conversation reveal what someone is thinking?
text:
What I built
Transcription and segmentation. Whisper transcribed the video; research assistants corrected it and tagged speakers. Splitting speaker turns into single utterances is the step most people skip, so I hand-coded 5,000 utterances, fine-tuned a segmentation model on them, and tested it on 500 held-out utterances: 96.8% agreement on boundaries.
Labeling what each utterance does. Each utterance was tagged as a question, a statement, a suggestion, an agreement, and so on, using four transformer models (DeepPavlov, RoBERTa, ConvBERT, DeBERTa) with a weighted vote that favors agreement among models over one model’s confidence. On 1,000 held-out utterances the vote scored 93.4%. Published single-model results on this task run from 85.8% to 91.6%.
Scoring similarity. Every utterance, every written guess, and every written thought became a sentence embedding (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). The outcome is the cosine similarity between an utterance and the guess or thought it was paired with. Small numbers, but consistent ones: study averages run from 0.11 to 0.18, with individual pairs ranging from about −0.2 to 0.9.
Modeling the shape over time. How similarity changes across a conversation was fit with Bayesian Gaussian process models (brms and Stan, Matérn 3/2 kernel), which let the data decide the shape of the curve. Each study was fit separately, then the curves were pooled with a random-effects meta-analysis that reports how much the studies disagree at every point. Six alternative prior settings and a smoother kernel were run on every model. The reasonable priors moved estimates by under 10%. The smoother kernel would not fit, and that is reported too.

title: Which parts of a conversation reveal what someone is thinking?
Which parts of a conversation reveal what someone is thinking?
text:
What this is good for
The pipeline is the product. It takes recorded conversation from any source, produces a validated utterance-level dataset with type labels, and fits a time-varying model with the uncertainty attached. The same code would run on user-interview recordings, support calls, or sales calls with the transcripts swapped in.
For user research, the suggestions result is the practical one. Analysis of an interview tends to center on how people answer the questions they were asked, yet the moments when someone volunteers a proposal (“it would be easier if…”) may say more about what they are thinking.
Two lessons carry over. Publish the holdout number next to every automated label; a 93% label and a 70% label should not enter a model the same way. And plan cluster sizes before collecting. These hierarchical models needed roughly 40 speakers per study to converge, ten times what this field usually records, and the study with 9 speakers had to be dropped from half the analyses. Sessions within users and calls within agents have the same constraint.

title: Which parts of a conversation reveal what someone is thinking?
text:
Limits
Similarity is not attention. The data show that guesses resemble recent speech; whether observers are consciously using it is an inference. The two interview-style studies had too few speakers to model on the speaker side, so the design differences visible in the first figure are mapped on the observer side only. The utterance types are broad; a finer scheme might sharpen or dissolve the suggestion result. If I ran this again I would fix the number of speakers per study before anything else, because that decided which questions could be asked at all.

title: Zach Schroeder
text:
Email  GitHub  LinkedIn  Scholar  Résumé


How do we use language to understand one another?
I’m a behavioral scientist and statistician with seven years of experience researching this question. In that time, I’ve built an analytic pipeline that transcribed and analyzed 20 years of video-recorded conversations to identify the best cues for understanding what someone is thinking; I examined partisanship and outrage in ~8.6 million tweets discussing “cancel culture,” including how outrage builds and fades in the weeks after a cancellation; and I ran three survey experiments on how students’ gender and sense of belonging shape the way they read ambiguous feedback.
If I’m not wrangling data at my desk, I’m deep in the woods with my dog.

title: Same sentence, different reader: how students interpret ambiguous feedback
text:
In brief. A professor tells a student, “This is a difficult major, many students do not persevere and instead drop out to study something easier.” Is that a warning or a vote of confidence? I ran three online studies (N = 1,125) in which students imagined hearing exactly that in office hours, then rated it, wrote about it, and picked next term’s classes. Men read the comment more positively than women in all three studies, including a preregistered replication that fixed its criteria for success before any data came in. Students who felt they belonged socially in their major read it more positively in two of the three. And students who read it more positively leaned toward the harder, more rewarding class.

title: Same sentence, different reader: how students interpret ambiguous feedback
text:
The problem
Research recommends feedback that is specific and actionable. Much of what people actually hear is a passing remark, and the reader fills in the meaning. Earlier work had found that men and women read explicitly negative feedback differently; almost nobody had tested the murky middle, which is where most real feedback lives. The same question comes up whenever an organization speaks to people in a sentence that could go either way: a status that reads “under review,” an error message, a policy notice.

title: Same sentence, different reader: how students interpret ambiguous feedback
text:
What I did
Study 1, exploratory (n = 423). Participants read the scenario and rated the comment on four items (how positive it was, how confident the professor seemed in them, how they felt afterward, and whether they would go back for more feedback; α = .89). They then chose between a difficult-but-fulfilling class and two easy ones, and completed scales for social belonging (feeling part of the major’s community) and intellectual belonging (confidence in their own ability). I fit a sequence of models and used what held up to write the hypotheses for Study 2.
Study 2, preregistered direct replication (n = 233). Same materials. Before collecting data I preregistered the hypotheses, a power analysis (at least 200 participants for .80 power), the exclusion rules, and what would count as success: each estimate had to land within one standard error of Study 1’s, and the model’s R² between .03 and .10.
Study 3, preregistered extension (n = 469). Added what the first two could not answer. Participants reported their imagined grade and their percentile standing in the major, rated each class option separately, and wrote about the conversation in their own words: a paragraph describing it, plus three words for how they would feel. Three research assistants coded every paragraph for how the writer saw themselves, the professor, and the interaction (inter-rater α = .76 to .88), and a sentiment dictionary scored the three-word answers.
All three studies ran in Qualtrics through the university participant pool under IRB approval.

Each dot is one study’s estimate with its 95% interval. The gold band is the success range set from Study 1 and written into the preregistration before Studies 2 and 3 were run. A filled dot landed inside it; an open dot did not. Left: how much more positively men rated the comment than women, on a 1 to 5 scale. Right: the change in rating for each point of social belonging. Hover for the numbers.

Gender replicated cleanly. Men rated the comment more positively than women in every study, by about 0.4 points on a five-point scale (average ratings of 2.09 to 2.60 for women and 2.52 to 3.04 for men), and all three estimates landed inside the preregistered range. The gap held after controlling for academic standing and for major (STEM, psychology, or other), which rules out the simplest explanation, that men just believed they were doing better.
Belonging replicated once, then fell short. Social belonging predicted a more positive reading in Studies 1 and 2, and Study 2’s estimate landed inside its range. In Study 3 the effect pointed the same way but was too small to meet the criterion. Study 3 ran in fall 2020, for many participants a first term spent entirely online, which may have changed what belonging to a major even meant. Intellectual belonging never predicted how the comment was read, although men reported more of it.
The open-text answers told the same story, with more detail. In their paragraphs, men described themselves and the interaction more positively than women did, and in their three-word answers they used fewer negative words for how they would feel. They did not describe the professor any differently. The difference sat in how readers saw themselves, not in how they judged the speaker, and a single rating could not have shown that.

title: Same sentence, different reader: how students interpret ambiguous feedback
text:
What this is good for
When wording is ambiguous, readers supply the meaning, and different groups of readers supply it differently and predictably. For anyone who writes the sentences people see in a portal, a letter, or an app, that means a message has to be tested on the people who will read it; the team that wrote it already knows what it was supposed to say. Pairing a quick rating with a short open-text prompt is cheap, and here it showed where the difference lived, which the rating alone could not.
The process carries over as well. Deciding before the data arrive what result would count as success (the sample size, the exclusions, the range of effects) is the same discipline a product team needs before reading an A/B test.

title: Same sentence, different reader: how students interpret ambiguous feedback
text:
Limits
One scenario, one sentence, and hypothetical class choices. There was no objective measure of ability, so I cannot say whether men over-read the comment or women under-read it. Participants were mostly first- and second-year students from a psychology subject pool, about 70% women; non-binary participants were too few to analyze separately and were excluded.

title: Moral and Partisan Differences in Cancel Culture Discourse
text: In brief. Opinions about cancel culture are everywhere online; data on it are scarce. I collected 8.6 million tweets about cancellations, inferred each author’s partisan lean from their bio, and scored every tweet for moral and emotional content with dictionaries and transformer classifiers. The result is the largest behavioral dataset on cancellation talk I have found, and it answers three questions any organization that listens to the public would ask: can you tell who is in a conversation without surveying them, how differently do the sides frame the same event, and how does the tone change as a story unfolds?

title: Moral and Partisan Differences in Cancel Culture Discourse
text:
Why this matters
“Cancel culture” gets invoked in newsrooms, legislatures, and product-policy meetings with total confidence and very little data. Underneath the punditry sit two questions that come up whenever an organization listens to the public: who is talking, and how are different groups framing the same thing? They are the same questions for a canceled celebrity, a product recall, or a nonprofit’s campaign. This project treats cancellation as a test case for answering them at scale.

title: Moral and Partisan Differences in Cancel Culture Discourse
text:
Data






Note



8,572,185 original English-language tweets from 4,035,488 users, collected through the Twitter Academic Research API in late 2022, deduplicated, retweets removed. Platform terms prohibit redistributing tweet or bio text, so no tweet, bio, or account is quoted or identified and every number here is an aggregate; the public figures who were the subjects of cancellations are named. The figures are computed live from small aggregate CSVs in the site repository; analysis code is at github.com/zjschroeder/Cancel-Culture-Text-Analysis.

title: Moral and Partisan Differences in Cancel Culture Discourse
text:
What I did
Partisan lean from a bio. Following Essig and DellaPosta (2024), 62 explicit partisan terms were split into a liberal and a conservative pole; the 1 to 9% of users with a term from one pole got a categorical lean. Every other bio term was scored by its TF-IDF cosine similarity to each pole, and each user’s continuous affiliation score is the weighted mean of their terms. That extends coverage to a third to a half of all users, at a measured cost: the continuous score agrees with the explicit labels at r = .28 to .43, an unsupervised scaling of the same bios recovers the labels at r = .13 to .44, and the partisan partition of the bio network is about as modular (Q = 0.13) as the published benchmark (0.17). Agreement with human coders is the check I have not run yet, so I quote no accuracy.
Moral content by triangulation. Each tweet was scored with the Moral Foundations Dictionary and its crowd-sourced extension, MoralBERT, Mformer, and TweetNLP’s RoBERTa emotion, offense, hate, irony, and sentiment classifiers. The outrage measure is where the dictionary’s and the transformer’s vice composites agree (r = .28 at the tweet level).
Topics. To see what people were talking about without imposing my own categories, I fit a 10-topic LDA model to the broad “cancel culture” sample (3.9 million tweets), choosing the number of topics by coherence, and compared it against BERTopic (clusters of sentence embeddings) and stLDA-C, a single-topic-per-tweet model built for short texts.
Event time. For the 57 academics, celebrities, and civilians with a datable cancellation, I aligned each target’s tweets to that target’s own peak-volume day and traced the outrage rate for 30 days on either side.

section: What this adds to interviews and surveys
text:
What this adds to interviews and surveys
People may describe a contested issue differently to a researcher than they do to each other. Interviews and surveys get the considered answer; a corpus like this one gets the unprompted one, from people who were never asked. The same scaffolding would run on open-text feedback (support tickets, portal comments, reviews): infer who is talking from how they describe themselves, compare how each group frames the same event, and watch how the tone shifts in the days after something goes wrong. Until the lean score is checked against human coders, it is best used to decide which questions an interview should ask.
